quests.instruction: Which noun form would you expect in Southern British English?
quests.hint: You have met this vowel in words like fast and mask. Does this word end in a similar cluster?
quests.explanation: Southern British /ˈkɒntrɑːst/ has the long vowel before /st/, while American /ˈkɑːntræst/ keeps the short one.
quests.dialectNote: The noun and verb forms differ in stress, but the vowel pattern is the same.

quests.instruction: Which version fits Southern British English?
quests.hint: Ignore the opening syllable and look at the stressed one.
quests.explanation: British /dɪˈzɑːstə/ has a long vowel before /st/.
quests.dialectNote: Not every long-vowel word is short, but this cluster is a reliable trigger.

quests.instruction: Which is more typical of Southern British English?
quests.hint: The consonant after the vowel is the voiced 'th'. Has that been a trigger before?
quests.explanation: In Southern British English the vowel in rather is long: /ˈrɑːðə/. General American has /ˈræðɚ/.
quests.dialectNote: Some words follow the pattern although the consonant is unusual.

quests.instruction: Which form does a Southern British speaker use? Beware of the family resemblance.
quests.hint: The word looks like class, but the suffix changes the pronunciation.
quests.explanation: Classic keeps a short vowel even in Southern British English, /ˈklæsɪk/. The -ic ending pulls it back, unlike in the base word class.
quests.dialectNote: Suffixes such as -ic often pull the vowel back to its short value.

quests.instruction: Which form is typical of Southern British?
quests.hint: This word contains /s/ after the vowel, like glass. Do you expect the same vowel?
quests.explanation: Passenger keeps the short vowel in British English, /ˈpæsɪndʒə/. Here the /s/ is followed by a vowel rather than a consonant, so the lengthening does not apply.
quests.dialectNote: It is one of the word-specific exceptions.

quests.instruction: Which form would many Southern British speakers use?
quests.hint: The suffix is -tic. Compare it with 'classic'.
quests.explanation: Fantastic has a short vowel in the stressed syllable: /fænˈtæstɪk/. It doesn't take the long vowel of 'fast'.
quests.dialectNote: Adding a suffix can change the vowel.

quests.instruction: Which respelling would many British speakers choose?
quests.hint: The stressed vowel is one you know from hot and job.
quests.explanation: Southern British has the rounded /ɒ/ in /ˈpɒlətɪks/.
quests.dialectNote: The pattern holds in longer words with stress on the first syllable.

quests.instruction: Which form fits General American?
quests.hint: Only the vowel is at stake here; the consonants are the same in both versions.
quests.explanation: American /ˈmɑːdl/ has the unrounded vowel /ɑ/. British /ˈmɒdl/ has the short rounded /ɒ/.
quests.dialectNote: The /d/ is identical in both, so only the vowel gives it away.

quests.instruction: Which form fits General American?
quests.hint: The first letter is silent in both varieties; only the vowel differs.
quests.explanation: American /ˈɑːnəst/ has /ɑː/. British /ˈɒnɪst/ has a short rounded vowel.
quests.dialectNote: Silent letters often hide that the vowel rule still applies.

quests.instruction: Which form is typical of British English?
quests.hint: In this word the vowel is followed by an 'r' in the spelling. How is it treated?
quests.explanation: British English has a short /ɒ/ before /r/, /ˈɒrɪndʒ/, and the /r/ starts the next syllable. Many Americans lengthen the vowel and colour it with /r/.
quests.dialectNote: Some Americans say 'AR-inj', so this is a tendency.

quests.instruction: Which form is British?
quests.hint: The vowel is followed by /r/ and a vowel in both versions.
quests.explanation: British /ˈfɒrɪst/ has a short vowel and a clear /r/ before the next vowel.
quests.dialectNote: The same short vowel appears in 'sorry' and 'moral'.

quests.instruction: Which form is more typical of British English?
quests.hint: Find the vowel before the double 'r'.
quests.explanation: British has the short /ɒ/: /ˈhɒrəbl/. American has /ˈhɔːrəbl/ or /ˈhɑːrəbl/.
quests.dialectNote: The vowel before intervocalic /r/ is short in British English.

quests.instruction: Which form shows the American tap?
quests.hint: The consonant lies between a stressed vowel and a weak syllable.
quests.explanation: American /ˈkæpɪɾl/ has a tapped /t/.
quests.dialectNote: You can now predict the tap in new words.

quests.instruction: Which version has the American tap?
quests.hint: Use what you learned about stress and consonants.
quests.explanation: The /t/ follows a stressed vowel and precedes a weak vowel, so it's tapped in General American.
quests.dialectNote: In British speech, this consonant may be a glottal stop.

quests.instruction: Which version is a General American tap?
quests.hint: Focus on the middle of the word.
quests.explanation: American /ˈaɪɾəm/ has a tap.
quests.dialectNote: You can hear the same effect in 'later' and 'meeting'.

quests.instruction: Which version is Southern British?
quests.hint: The consonant before the vowel may have a glide after it.
quests.explanation: British keeps /j/ after /n/: /ˈnjuːtrəl/. American drops it.
quests.dialectNote: The position of the /j/ is predictable: after /n/, /t/, /d/, /s/, /z/.

quests.instruction: Which version is General American?
quests.hint: This word has a familiar pattern after /d/.
quests.explanation: American drops /j/ after /d/: /ɪnˈdʊr/. British has /ɪnˈdjʊə/.
quests.dialectNote: Some British speakers may say 'en-DOR' in casual speech.

quests.instruction: Which form matches Southern British?
quests.hint: The glide can appear after /st/ as well.
quests.explanation: British /ˈstjuːpɪd/ has the glide. American /ˈstuːpɪd/ does not.
quests.dialectNote: The cluster /st/ behaves like /t/ in this respect.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of rhotic accents?
quests.hint: Look for the r-colouring of the vowel.
quests.explanation: Rhotic /ˈnɝvəs/ has an r-coloured vowel. Non-rhotic /ˈnɜːvəs/ has a plain long vowel.
quests.dialectNote: The same pattern applies in words like 'nervous', 'perfect' and 'certain'.

quests.instruction: Which form is typical of General American?
quests.hint: In this word the ending changes together with the first vowel.
quests.explanation: American /ˈθɝoʊ/ has an r-coloured vowel and a full ending. British /ˈθʌrə/ has a short vowel and a weak ending.
quests.dialectNote: Words with 'ough' show the range of English spelling.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of Southern British?
quests.hint: Three features are combined: a vowel, an /r/ and a consonant.
quests.explanation: British /ˈkɒnsət/ has a rounded vowel and no /r/. American /ˈkɑːnsɚt/ has an unrounded vowel and an /r/.
quests.dialectNote: The vowel and the /r/ give two separate clues.

quests.instruction: Which stress pattern is typical of Southern British English?
quests.hint: French loanwords may have a different stress in each dialect.
quests.explanation: British /ˈdebriː/ has first-syllable stress; American /dəˈbriː/ has second-syllable stress.
quests.dialectNote: This is the same French-loan pattern as 'ballet'.

quests.instruction: Which version is more likely in British English?
quests.hint: The word can be a noun. Think about the stress in the noun.
quests.explanation: British /rɪˈses/ is stressed on the second syllable; American often stresses the first: /ˈriːsɛs/.
quests.dialectNote: The American form is common for school recess.

quests.instruction: Which form is more common in American English?
quests.hint: Consider where the strongest beat falls.
quests.explanation: American /frʌnˈtɪr/ often stresses the last syllable, while British /ˈfrʌntɪə/ stresses the first.
quests.dialectNote: Both forms are used in both countries.

quests.instruction: Which form is British?
quests.hint: This is a lexical pair. It's one of the words you have to know.
quests.explanation: British /ˈliːvə/ has a long vowel. American /ˈlɛvɚ/ has a short one.
quests.dialectNote: Some Americans use the long vowel.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of American English?
quests.hint: One consonant may be missing.
quests.explanation: American /ˈsɑːdɚ/ omits /l/; British /ˈsɒldə/ or /ˈsəʊldə/ includes it.
quests.dialectNote: Lexical differences may involve silent letters.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of Southern British English?
quests.hint: Which vowel matches the nasal cluster?
quests.explanation: British /ɑːnt/ has the long vowel. American commonly has /ænt/, though /ɑnt/ occurs in some regions.
quests.dialectNote: Regional exceptions exist in New England and the South.

quests.instruction: Which version is Southern British?
quests.hint: Plural forms follow the pattern of the base word.
quests.explanation: The plural keeps the long vowel of glass.
quests.dialectNote: This shows that inflected forms follow their base.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of non-rhotic speech?
quests.hint: An r before a consonant is at play.
quests.explanation: Non-rhotic /ˈfɑːməsi/ has a long vowel and no /r/.
quests.dialectNote: Healthcare vocabulary often shows the difference.

quests.instruction: Which form is typical of Southern British English?
quests.hint: Listen to the second syllable.
quests.explanation: British /ˈlæptɒp/ has a rounded vowel. American /ˈlæptɑːp/ has an unrounded one.
quests.dialectNote: Even compound words follow the pattern.
